opus-5.5.text:
I think 2023 will be remembered as the year large language models went mainstream. ChatGPT had come out at the very end of 2022, but 2023 was when it really permeated public consciousness. Suddenly everyone, my neighbors, people in government, students, was using these systems and forming opinions about them. Then we saw GPT-4, Claude, Llama, and a whole wave of open models, and the pace felt dizzying.

I also think it will be remembered as the year the conversation about AI risk and governance exploded. We had the open letters calling for a pause, the statements about extinction risk, the White House executive order, the UK AI Safety Summit, and progress on the EU AI Act. Some of that was overheated, frankly, but it put these questions on the policy agenda in a way that hadn't happened before.

From a research perspective, my own view is a bit more measured. These systems are remarkable at producing fluent text, and they encode a surprising amount of knowledge. But they're not reliable. They hallucinate, they don't know what they don't know, and they lack the kind of grounded, updatable knowledge representation we'd want in a trustworthy system. So I hope 2023 will also be seen as the year we started to take seriously the engineering work needed to make these models dependable: better uncertainty quantification, retrieval and grounding, separating factual knowledge from linguistic competence, and building systems that can say "I'm not sure."

So my short answer: 2023 was the year AI arrived for the general public. The question for the next few years is whether we can turn that excitement into systems that actually deserve people's trust.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT permeated public consciousness and that large language models went mainstream in 2023, but it does not communicate that ChatGPT's impact was global.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think 2023 will be remembered as the year that large language models went mainstream, obviously. ChatGPT came out at the very end of 2022, and then 2023 was the year everybody—the public, policymakers, every company—suddenly had to reckon with what these systems could and couldn't do. From a research standpoint, I think it will be remembered as the year we really started to understand the limitations of these systems, not just the capabilities. Early in the year there was a lot of excitement, maybe even hype, about emergent abilities and sparks of general intelligence. And by the end of the year I think a more sober picture had set in: these models are extraordinarily good at certain kinds of linguistic tasks, but they hallucinate, they lack a reliable world model, their knowledge is frozen at training time, and they have real trouble knowing what they don't know.

I've been arguing for a while that we're asking a single artifact—the language model—to do too many jobs at once. It's supposed to be the knowledge base, the reasoning engine, the dialog manager, and the user interface all rolled into one set of weights. And a lot of the problems we saw in 2023 stem from that. So I think one of the legacies of 2023 is that it pushed the field toward thinking about architectures where the language model is one component, surrounded by retrieval, tools, verification, and ways to update knowledge without retraining.

The other thing I'd point to is that 2023 was the year AI safety and governance moved from a niche conversation to a mainstream one. We had the open letters, the congressional hearings, the executive order in the U.S., the EU AI Act advancing, the UK summit. Some of that was driven by concerns I think are overstated, and some by concerns I think are quite legitimate, particularly around misuse and around deploying unreliable systems in high-stakes settings. But either way, the fact that governments took it seriously is something people will look back on.

So if I had to summarize: 2023 was the year of the LLM, both the triumph and the beginning of the reckoning.

r001.rationale: The response says 2023 was when large language models went mainstream and that the public, policymakers, and companies broadly had to reckon with them, linking this shift to ChatGPT.

astra-6.text:
I think 2023 will be remembered as the year that large language models really entered public awareness. People who had never thought much about AI could suddenly interact with a system in ordinary language and discover that it could do a remarkable range of things.

What’s particularly interesting is the gap between that breadth of capability and its reliability. These systems can produce a beautiful explanation, write useful code, and then make a very basic mistake—or confidently invent something. So we have this exciting new technology, but we’re still figuring out how to characterize its limits and how to use it responsibly.

I think we’ll look back on 2023 as an inflection point in adoption and experimentation. Whether it was also the decisive scientific turning point is something we’ll need more distance to judge.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes large language models entering public awareness in 2023, but does not clearly identify ChatGPT or say it achieved widespread global impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think 2023 will be remembered as the year that large language models really entered public consciousness. ChatGPT gave people a very direct way to experience what these systems could do, and that changed the conversation about AI. Suddenly, people across all kinds of professions were asking how this technology might affect their work.

From a research perspective, what’s striking is the breadth of capabilities that emerge from training a model to predict the next token. But there’s still a substantial gap between producing convincing language and being reliably correct. These systems can be very useful, and then make mistakes that are difficult for a user to recognize.

So I think we’ll remember both the excitement and the realization that we have a lot of work to do on reliability, evaluation, and understanding when we should trust these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT brought large language models into public consciousness, changed the AI conversation, and prompted people across professions to consider its effects—clearly conveying widespread impact.
